chapter_theme: The closing summary (கட்டுரை) of the Vanchi book: one sentence lists what the book set out about the Chera line, rulers of the west (its righteousness, valour and strength, its old city, festivals, the gods' visits, the wealth and grain of its land, its vari and kuravai songs), and says the book lies viewed as one with Senguttuvan, whose army of true swords fought in keeping with aram, drove back the sea and reached the bank of the Ganga.

silappathikaram:vanchi_kandam_katturai:1.reading: The narrator closes the Vanchi book by gathering into one view the righteousness, valour and strength of those born in the garlanded Chera line who rule the west among the three crowned kings, the excellence of their old city of ancient victories, its festivals and divine visitors, the wealth of the families and the plenty of grain in their land of unbroken joy, and the vari and kuravai songs, all seen together with Senguttuvan, whose army of unfailing swords completed the deeds of war joined to righteousness, who drove back the sea and went to the bank of the great Ganga, and declares the book complete.
silappathikaram:vanchi_kandam_katturai:1.nuance: Lines 4 to 8 repeat the frame that closes the Puhar and Madurai books, but the frame is cut short: there is no river and no unfailing sky here, and the arts shrink to the vari and kuravai (line 9), the hill-folk's and herders' songs of this book. Where the Madurai summary ends on a king's death, this one adds a phrase of its own, அறத்தொடு பொருந்திய மறத்துறை (lines 10 to 11), valour 'fitted to aram', and makes war the book's centre. The summary names neither Kannaki nor the Pattini stone for which the march to the north was made (25:113-130); it keeps only the king, his sea and the Ganga. கடல்பிறக் கோட்டி (line 12) is the epithet under which the Patitruppattu's fifth decad names Senguttuvan (கடல் பிறக்கோட்டிய செங்குட்டுவன்); the shared epithet is the Tamil's ground for taking the epic's king as the decad's patron, not proof that the two portraits are one man's history.

claims.claim: a king's warfare can be waged in keeping with righteousness

links.note: Senguttuvan rejects a stone from the Podiyil hill bathed in the Kaveri as unworthy of those born in his line of valour, and resolves that if the Himalaya's king will not give a stone to carve the great Pattini goddess, he will march north; the summary views the book as one with the king whose army fought with valour fitted to aram and reached the Ganga.
links.teaches: The king's own reason for the northern war was the honour of his line of valour, with the goddess's stone as its occasion, and the summary keeps exactly that reason and drops the occasion, so the book that began with worship for Kannaki is remembered as a Chera conquest called righteous.

links.note: Both summaries open with the same frame (aram, maram, the old city, festivals, the gods' visits, the land's wealth); the Madurai summary keeps the river and the unfailing sky and ends with the Pandya who lay dead on his throne-couch with his chaste queen, the Vanchi summary drops river and sky and ends with Senguttuvan's army at the Ganga, adding valour fitted to aram.
links.teaches: The shared frame lets the difference show: the Pandya book is summed up in a king undone by a wrong verdict, the Chera book in a king whose war is declared righteous, so the epic's last word on aram passes from the court of justice to the battlefield, and neither summary names the woman both books turn on.

links.note: The preface to the fifth decad names Senguttuvan, who drove back the sea, as the king who went north to take a stone for the goddess Pattini, defeated the Aryan lord and bathed it in the Ganga; the epic's summary names him by the same epithet (கடல்பிறக் கோட்டி) and the same Ganga, and says nothing of the stone.
links.teaches: The decad's preface and the epic's summary give the same king the same two marks, the sea driven back and the Ganga reached, but only the Sangam preface keeps the Pattini stone as the purpose of the march, so the epic, which tells the stone's story at length, lets its own summary remember the expedition as the preface's bare royal conquest.

gains.a: the summary's epithet gains its source: கடல்பிறக் கோட்டி is the name under which a Patitruppattu decad was sung for this king, which shows the summary closing the book in the older praise-poets' terms
gains.b: the preface's brief clause on the Pattini stone gains the epic's full account of why and for whom the stone was sought, and a case where the epic's own closing formula leaves that clause out

source_issues: Line 7 reads அவருறை நாட்டுக் where the Madurai summary has அவருடை நாட்டுக்; line 14 reads ஒருபரிசு நோக்கிக் where the Madurai summary has ஒருபரிசா நோக்கிக். Either may be a variant or a misprint; the sense is unaffected.
Line 15 (கிடந்த வஞ்சிக் காண்ட முற்றிற்று) joins the closing participle of the sentence to the colophon, so the colophon is marked as part of the unit, as in the Madurai summary.
